articles.headline: Melania Trump secures $7.2M for foster care scholarships at LSU ahead of Alabama showdown
keyFacts: First lady Melania Trump announced a $7.2 million scholarship endowment at Louisiana State University for young Americans with foster care experience.
The permanent endowment includes a $5 million commitment from MMR Group and $2.2 million raised from 75 LSU Foundation donors, university officials said.
The initiative was highlighted during LSU's football game against Alabama with on-field presentations, custom merchandise, and stadium recognition.
body: BATON ROUGE, La. — First lady Melania Trump announced a $7.2 million scholarship endowment at Louisiana State University (LSU) on Saturday, delivering a message of hope to young Americans who have experienced foster care before receiving a special football tribute ahead of the Tigers' rivalry showdown against Alabama.

Trump wore a Dalma suede bomber jacket by Nour Hammour, paired with an Adam Lippes skirt and Manolo Blahnik BB pumps for the occasion, blending her signature polished style with a more relaxed look suited to a college football weekend.

The first lady's visit unfolded against a distinctly LSU backdrop, with purple-and-gold tailgating crowds lining the motorcade route and a massive American flag hanging above the stage inside Patrick F. Taylor Hall.
LSU cheerleaders flanked Trump during her remarks, and the Tiger mascot presented her with both scholarship checks while wearing a signature "Be Best" T-shirt.
MELANIA TRUMP CHALLENGES CONGRESS TO MAKE HER FOSTER CARE EXECUTIVE ORDER PERMANENT LAW: 'THEIR BIRTHRIGHT'
There, university officials, donors and students gathered for an announcement supporting young Americans who have experienced foster care through Trump's " Fostering the Future " initiative.
"This achievement will give young people from foster care an anchor of stability, a strong educational foundation, and a chance to build a wonderful life," Trump told attendees.
The permanent endowment includes a $5 million commitment from MMR Group, led by LSU alumnus James B. "Pepper" Rutland, and an additional $2.2 million raised from 75 LSU Foundation donors.
LSU Foundation President and CEO Krista Raney said the contributions had brought the scholarship fund to "more than $7.2 million and growing."
LSU President Wade Rousse said the $5 million leadership gift is expected to generate approximately $200,000 annually, helping students cover tuition, fees, books and room and board.
ED ORGERON-LANE KIFFIN PAIRING ALREADY PAYING DIVIDENDS FOR LSU TIGERS DURING PIVOTAL RECRUITING WEEKEND
"At LSU, we believe talent is everywhere, but we understand that opportunity is not," Rousse said.
The university also embraced the occasion with several football-themed gifts for the first lady.
Trump received a custom purple-and-gold LSU jersey bearing the name "MELANIA" and the number 14, along with a Tigers helmet featuring her BE BEST Fostering the Future logo.
Former LSU coach Ed Orgeron, known to fans as Coach O, joined the presentation with a specially designed commemorative football created by Big Game USA, a company owned by LSU alumnus Chris Calandra.

The initiative extended beyond the ceremony, with special patches on LSU players' jerseys, helmet decals, cheerleader uniforms, mascot attire and commemorative fan towels, according to the White House .
COLLEGE FOOTBALL'S FIRST FULL SATURDAY IS HERE AND IT'S A CELEBRATION OF AMERICA AT ITS BEST
The celebration continued at Tiger Stadium, where the first lady's Fostering the Future initiative received a special on-field recognition during LSU's highly anticipated matchup against Alabama.

Students joined LSU's Mike the Tiger mascot and others on the field for a ceremonial check presentation highlighting the $7.2 million scholarship endowment. Trump also appeared on the stadium's massive Jumbotron as fans cheered and chants of "USA" echoed through the stadium.
The game-day atmosphere included a military flyover above Tiger Stadium, adding to the spectacle as thousands of fans gathered for the SEC rivalry.
The first lady's visit extended beyond the scholarship announcement, with LSU incorporating Fostering the Future branding into players' jerseys, helmets and other game-day elements.
A special Melania Trump challenge coin was also designated for the game's opening coin toss, according to the White House.
The legendary LSU-Alabama rivalry even found its way into the scholarship announcement.
After Trump revealed that LSU has 14 Fostering the Future scholars compared with Alabama's nine, Raney offered a lighthearted observation.
"Mrs. Trump, what I heard you say is that LSU has 14 scholarship recipients and Alabama has nine," Raney said. "So I think that means we've already won the first point."
Trump told attendees that 26 universities nationwide are supporting 100 Fostering the Future scholars this semester.
"While most eyes will be on the athletes today, I encourage you to recognize LSU's Fostering the Future scholars, who are just as remarkable," she said.
Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry , Louisiana first lady Sharon Landry and House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., were among those in attendance.
Trump also received a handcrafted wooden bowl made from a fallen limb of one of LSU's historic oak trees, a gift symbolizing the lasting impact of the scholarship initiative.
Fostering the Future, launched in 2021 as part of Trump's BE BEST initiative , seeks to expand educational opportunities for young people who have experienced foster care.
"A great education does more than prepare someone for work life," Trump said. "It gives something no one can ever take away."
She closed with an encouraging message to scholarship recipients.
"To the Fostering the Future scholars here today, and throughout America: I see you. I believe in you. And I will keep working to create new opportunities with you," she said.

articles.headline: Lando Norris claims F1 São Paulo GP pole as ‘crazy’ rain disrupts qualifying
keyFacts: McLaren driver Lando Norris claimed pole position for the São Paulo Grand Prix after navigating heavy rain that disrupted qualifying.
A host of drivers received grid penalties, including Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, resulting in a mixed-up starting formation for the race.
More rain is predicted for the Sunday race, leaving the grid wide open from front to back.
body: Mastering the most treacherous of conditions at Interlagos, Lando Norris had the edge to take pole position for McLaren at the São Paulo Grand Prix, having bested a downpour that tested every driver. But with more rain predicted for the race on Sunday, it remains wide open from the front to the very back of the grid.

After a qualifying session that took two and a half hours to complete because of delays caused by the heavy rain, Norris came out on top but the grid will be marked by a very mixed-up formation, as a host of drivers took penalties.

“We could just have an exciting race with a little bit of everything, honestly,” he said. “I was certainly more confident in the wet and inter [intermediate] than I was in the dry. I think in the dry we just didn’t have the pace, so I’ll be certainly more happy if I wake up and see rain in the morning.”

Mercedes’ George Russell was second on track but the British driver has a grid penalty, promoting his teammate Kimi Antonelli, the new world champion, to second and Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson to third, with Audi’s Nico Hülkenberg up to fourth.

Interlagos was awash with streams of water flooding across the track so the early runs were a real test. Russell called the conditions “crazy”. “I love driving in the rain. I love driving in the rain here but if that was a race there was no way we should be driving in that,” he said. “Because the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident is very, very high.”

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton were also among a raft of drivers receiving a grid penalty for taking a new engine and the Dutchman opted not to set a time after Q1, to save his tyres for the race, and will start from 21st.

Hamilton also had to take a full range of engine components: having had a new internal combustion engine (ICE) for final practice, that then suffered a problem and he will start from 20th. His Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc finished in fourth but has a 10-place penalty for taking a new ICE and will start from 14th.

Those penalties put Mercedes in a prime position to close out the constructors’ championship on Sunday. They will clinch the title if they outscore Ferrari by three points in Brazil. With their having secured the drivers’ championship with Antonelli last weekend, it will be their first double since 2020 and their ninth constructors’ title.

Russell has a five-place penalty for taking a new engine and he will start from seventh but he was left furious with his team that he was told by the team to back off on his last quick run, which he felt was enough to have at least set the best time.
“That was definitely the pole lap,” he said. “Misjudgment on our side, we need to understand what happened. The rain was coming and we should’ve just finished the lap.”

For McLaren this was the result they were looking for having brought what was expected to be the last of their major upgrades to this race, with the focus on a new front wing. They are hoping the developments – which are designed looking toward their 2027 car with the intent of addressing the narrow edge of balance of the current model – would prove beneficial and Norris had noted he felt they were working.
“For the team, it’s reassuring for them, it’s a confidence booster for all of them to end the season knowing we’ve caught up a lot since the beginning of the season,” he said.
Quite what awaits on Sunday remains very much up in the air, however, and no driver can be ruled out if the rain does return.

Verstappen will not consider the cause lost at the Autódromo José Carlos Pace, where he has shown superb form in the past. Rain is expected for the race set for 5pm on Sunday. In 2016 he came back from 16th to third in the wet, last year he also took third after starting from the pit lane and in 2024 he won from 17th on the grid.

Hamilton has similar form in Brazil having come back twice in the same weekend in 2021, from 20th to fifth in the sprint and then from 10th to the win in the race. However, he likely faces a far tougher task this time round, with the Ferrari’s power deficit looking exposed at Interlagos, though that deficit would be somewhat negated if the race is wet.

Rafael Câmara, the Brazilian Ferrari junior driver replacing Esteban Ocon at Haas for the rest of this season and with a full-time drive next year, had made a good showing on his F1 debut at his home grand prix by making it into Q2, but he then crashed out late on, ending the session.
Cadillac’s Sergio Pérez also took a full set of new engine components and he will start from the back of the grid.

articles.headline: What we know so far after Polish gunman opens fire in Krakow main square
keyFacts: Six people were killed and sixteen injured after a gunman opened fire in Krakow's main square before being arrested, officials said.
A minister said early investigations indicate the arrested 25-year-old Polish suspect was inspired by far-right ideologies.
Krakow's mayor declared a mourning period until November 11, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk is scheduled to give an address.
body: - Published

At least six people have been killed and several others injured after a gunman suspected to have ties to the far-right opened fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland. Here's everything we know so far.
How did the attack unfold?
The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, the bustling central point of the city.
Police said a man drove into the square before beginning to fire "at random people from his car".
Footage from the scene shows scenes of panic as people fled, with the sound of gunfire clearly heard.
A passing tram was shot at during the apparently random attack, shattering windows but no passengers were injured.
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the attacker, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.
The gunman was shot but is alive and has been arrested.
Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment a police officer confronts the suspect on the ground before firing his weapon several times.
The officer then falls to the ground, apparently having been injured himself.
Shop windows in the square have signs of damage, seemingly from bullets, with glass shards scattered along the floor.
City officials have urged people who live in the city and tourists to stay away from the area while an investigation continues.
How many people have died and been injured?
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed, including a foreign national.
Sixteen people, including five foreigners and the attacker, were taken to hospital. Among those being treated are two police officers who were shot while detaining the attacker.

One of the police officers was described as being in a "very critical condition" by a Polish government minister after being shot three times while arresting the attacker. The officer is undergoing surgery, he added.
Polish authorities have not confirmed the names and ages of the other victims.
What do we know about the suspect and motive?
Police have identified the attacker as a 25-year-old Polish man but have not confirmed his name.
The suspect was wearing "military-style attire" and had a military-grade weapon, according to a police spokesperson. However, authorities have confirmed the attacker was not a soldier.
"Many pieces of weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle", the spokesperson added.
Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.
A minister has said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.
His home is being searched with support from counter-terrorism police.
How did witnesses describe the attack?
The shooting happened in one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, a busy location which is also a popular tourist destination.
Jonathan Balshaw from Ipswich was there with his Polish girlfriend Dominika. The couple were outside St Mary's Basilica, in the corner of the square, when the shooting started.
Jonathan said: "We ran down the side of the church and through the side door and hid with several other people until the gunfire died down.
"A lot of shots were fired, more than 20 with it sounding like multiple different firearms - there were two distinctly different noises."
Caitlin Shasby from Newcastle arrived in Krakow yesterday with her friend Jon for a long weekend.
She said they heard shots from their hotel room but were not sure what was happening until their hotel rang them and told them to "stay in our rooms until further notice".
What has the reaction been in Poland and internationally?
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk is on his way to Krakow and is expected to give an address later on Saturday.
Earlier, he said he was being kept informed by the interior minister and that police were investigating "the background and all the circumstances".
Krakow Mayor Åukasz GibaÅa has signed an order declaring a period of mourning in the city which will last until Wednesday, November 11.
President Karol Nawrocki said he was "deeply concerned" and was awaiting "a full explanation of the circumstances surrounding these tragic events".
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose described it as a "savage and murderous attack".
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the shooting was "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland".

articles.headline: Star Wars Zero Company studio Bit Reactor lays off staff, a month after bringing furloughed developers back
keyFacts: Developer Bit Reactor has laid off an unspecified number of staff members.
The layoffs occurred one month after the studio brought some previously furloughed developers back to work following the launch of Star Wars Zero Company.
Bit Reactor has not disclosed the total number of employees affected by these recent job cuts.
body: Star Wars Zero Company developer Bit Reactor has laid off an unspecified number of staff, a month after bringing some of its furloughed team back to work.
Several developers announced on LinkedIn on Friday, 6th November, that they had been let go, as first reported by Bespin Bulletin. Bit Reactor hasn't said how many people are affected.

Among them is senior environment artist Ryan Lopez, who spent three and a half years working on Zero Company, from pre-production to launch, and was laid off after a three-month furlough. UI engineer Tyler Eichten, who worked on much of the on-screen UI for the game's tactical missions, and Ryan Mosher from the QA team have also confirmed they were let go.
"While it stings, I'm really proud of what we built together," Lopez wrote. "It was a privilege to ship a game with you."

Bit Reactor furloughed most of its staff in the weeks before Zero Company launched on 27th August, with one source putting the figure at roughly 80 percent. The studio appeared to have run out of money just short of release.

The game did well regardless, and is thought to have sold more than a million copies within a month. Then, in a message shared on Bluesky on 7th October, CEO Greg Foertsch said the studio had "started the process of returning more of our team back to work". Asking staff to step away so close to launch was "an incredibly difficult decision", he said, "but one that was necessary to help us eventually bring as many people back as possible".
It's thought more than half the studio returned, though not everyone went back on full pay. It's not clear whether any of those who returned were among the people laid off this week.

In Eurogamer's Star Wars Zero Company review, we awarded the game four out of five stars, saying, "an already winning genre is matched with the perfect setting in this earnest, heartfelt, smart and slightly ramshackle turn-based tactics gem".

articles.headline: The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance
keyFacts: A reviewer tested the $249 UV-tracking necklace called Gem, which measures UVA and UVB radiation separately using a small pendant and a mobile app.
The reviewer experienced heat exhaustion under a patio umbrella, leading them to discover via the app that UV radiation penetrates shade and that a medication increased their heat sensitivity.
The reviewer found the device helped them balance sun protection with vitamin D intake, though they noted fluctuating countdown timers and high costs.
body: With temperatures rising to the 90s in Los Angeles, avoiding the heat wasn’t exactly an option while I was at a relative’s outdoor party in August. So I sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan nearby, figuring I was protected from the sun and heat. Half an hour later, I felt exhausted, dizzy, nauseous, and generally unwell, symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion.
The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance
What started as a test to understand how sun exposure was aging my skin took a turn that I wasn’t expecting.

Around the same time, I received a notification from an app used by the $249 ($149 at the time of publication) UV-tracking necklace I’d been wearing, called Gem, from a company called The90. It warned that my UV exposure had climbed considerably. It turns out UV radiation wasn’t repelled by this patio umbrella, and it’s hard to ever be fully protected because radiation can be reflected or scattered by objects in the environment. While UV exposure and overheating are different things, I’d mistakenly assumed the shade and the fan would adequately protect me from both.

This led to a discovery: One of my medications increases my sensitivity to heat, which helped to explain similar episodes I’d experienced over the years. The Gem didn’t diagnose anything, but it prompted me to investigate something I might otherwise have dismissed. Since then, I’ve been more mindful about limiting time outdoors during hours of peak heat and UV, staying hydrated, and paying closer attention to how I’m feeling outside.

I’ll admit my initial interest in tracking UV was largely vanity-driven. As much as I try to challenge harmful beauty standards, I’m hardly immune to them. Having started going gray in my 20s, I’m keen on slowing down other visible signs of aging where I reasonably can. But between being Indian (I rarely get sunburned thanks in part to my skin’s higher melanin content, not that it eliminates the risk of sun damage or skin cancer) and living within walking distance of the beach in perpetually sunny LA, I hadn’t given much thought to how much UV exposure I was actually getting. The Gem has helped me better understand it by providing a range of estimates, some more useful than others.

The included UV-detecting sensor measures UVA and UVB radiation separately, rather than simply displaying my area’s UV forecast. UVB is primarily responsible for sunburn and helps your skin produce vitamin D, while UVA contributes to premature aging, even when you aren’t visibly burning. Thankfully, getting these metrics doesn’t come at the cost of wearing a bulky device. The circular pendant comes with a cute, thin necklace I’d happily wear even if it didn’t track anything. Its titanium, gold- or silver-colored chain pairs well with a variety of outfits. Battery life lasted almost exactly a week (the advertised lifespan), and the Gem recharges using an included charging dock. The90 plans to release a hat clip and bag tag early next year, which seem ideal for those who prefer not to wear it around their neck.

The mobile app is central to the experience. It has easy-to-read graphs and jargon-light explanations. I enjoyed using it. While not required, you can create a skin profile so that it can estimate a range of metrics based on the sensor’s UVA and UVB readings. The profile is based upon factors like skin type, sensitivities, clothing, and sunscreen. That means its estimates aren’t based on UV exposure alone, though they’re still predictions rather than direct measurements of how your body is responding to sunlight.

There’s a lot here, including your estimated vitamin D production, potential circadian light benefits, estimated nitric oxide-related benefits, cumulative UVA exposure, and recent accumulated UVA exposure. Alongside cumulative UVA exposure and weekly trends, its Skin Aging Zone assesses potential aging-related risk and offers personalized skincare advice. It also provides a personalized sunburn countdown, sunscreen reminders, and a daily Sun Score.

The Sun Score is a rating that incorporates various metrics to balance sunlight’s potential benefits against the risks of overexposure. The company encourages users to aim for a daily Sun Score of 90, though more sun isn’t necessarily better. Too little exposure means missing potential benefits, while excessive UV can damage your skin. I appreciated the context, but the individual estimated measurements proved more revealing than the Sun Score.

The UV readings in the app responded quickly as I moved between sunlight, shade, and indoors, even registering changes near windows. I couldn’t independently verify the sensor’s accuracy, but the readings behaved as expected as I shifted between environments. However, there were times when I noticed the Gem sometimes failed to register that I had been outside. Eventually, I discovered the app needs to remain running in the background (at least on iPhone; I haven’t tested on Android), as measurements aren’t stored on the sensor, and fully closing the app interrupts tracking.

My experience at the outdoor party challenged my assumptions about how much protection I was getting from the shade. Just as surprising to me was learning how little UVB I accumulated during a typical week, despite living somewhere so sunny. I fell short of the app’s estimated sunlight-derived vitamin D target almost daily, prompting me to research how melanin, while offering some natural UV protection, impacts vitamin D production from sunlight. Until then, I’d mostly thought about sun exposure in terms of protecting my skin from damage. Seeing how little UVB I was accumulating made me consider what I might be missing out on, too.

The vitamin D countdown wasn’t as helpful as I had hoped. During one test, its estimate of how much additional sunlight I needed dropped from several hours to under an hour, then climbed past six hours just minutes later. The fluctuations appeared related to changing UVB intensity, though I couldn’t verify that. I noticed similar fluctuations in the app’s estimated time to sunburn. With both countdowns changing so dramatically, I stopped paying much attention to the exact times and focused instead on the broader picture: whether it felt like I was getting too much or too little sun.

That was perhaps the biggest surprise of testing the Gem. After my experience using it at the outdoor party in August, I’d expected it just would encourage me to spend less time in the sun each day. In reality, my exposure often falls at one of two extremes: either too little to meet the app’s estimated targets or enough to raise concerns about overexposure, even when I thought I was protected by the shade.

I now try to be more mindful about my UV exposure, even when I’m not using the Gem. I try to limit time spent outdoors during peak UV hours, and I try to get some sunlight on days spent mostly indoors. I credit the Gem with helping me better understand how my time outside could affect my well-being in ways I’d never considered, though the usefulness of your findings may vary.

At $249 outside of a deal, it’s expensive, though it’s nice that it doesn’t have a subscription. I personally can’t justify the price given how much time I spend indoors, but I see the appeal for people who spend considerable time outside, or those who want to be more mindful of sun protection. For the price, I wish the app’s guidance was clearer at times, and I wish it could track UV without the app being open in the background, but the Gem ultimately got me thinking less about how my body looks and more about how I’m treating it.
Photography by Sheena Vasani / The Verge

articles.headline: The Best GTA Alternatives For Kids And Families
keyFacts: GameSpot published a list of ten family-friendly video game alternatives to Grand Theft Auto VI for children and parents to play together.
The list includes open-world and exploration titles such as Lego City Undercover, Forza Horizon, Little Kitty, Big City, and No Man's Sky.
Other suggested games include chaotic or sandbox experiences like Untitled Goose Game, Goat Simulator 3, and Mario Kart World.
body: Grand Theft Auto VI is going to be the biggest video game launch of all time, and it's not particularly close. Millions and millions of people are eagerly awaiting their chance to start up the game on Xbox or PlayStation and sink hundreds (or more) hours into Leonida, but there is a very large demographic that Rockstar's game doesn't target: families with kids.

GTA 6 is filled with drugs, murder, sex, and pretty much everything else you could think to put in the ESRB rating description for a video game. That means you probably aren't letting your kids play it (seriously, please don't), but there's a good chance they're going to experience some FOMO--especially if they hear other kids at school are playing it (though those kids are probably lying).

So, with that in mind, it's a good idea to have some GTA alternatives ready to go, not only so your kids have something fun to play, but also so you can enjoy a game together. Below are 10 great Grand Theft Auto VI alternatives for kids and families, ranging from games that play like "baby's first GTA" to games that take one element of Rockstar's series and run with it … and one bizarre, family-friendly game that Rockstar happened to make itself.
Lego City Undercover (PS4, Xbox One, Switch, Wii U, PC)

Of any game on this list, Lego City Undercover is the one that most resembles Grand Theft Auto in its structure, with access to a big open world and vehicles to drive. Because it's a family-friendly game, however, you play as police officer Chase McCain rather than a hardened criminal, with a particular focus on detective work as you investigate crimes throughout the city. It supports two-person cooperative play, and because there are a whole bunch of movie references intended for parents rather than kids--unless you've shown them Shawshank Redemption already--you may want to pick up the second controller yourself.
See at Steam
Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight (PS5, Xbox Series X|S, Switch 2, PC)

If you're looking for an open-world alternative to GTA that puts a little more emphasis on combat, then Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight is a great choice. Mixing the dark, brooding tone you'd expect from Batman with a bunch of the Lego games' silly gags, its structure opens up after the first few hours, letting you glide around the city or speed down the streets in the Batmobile. What really helps it stand out, however, is the combat, which plays like a simplified take on the Arkham games' system that sees Batman effortlessly comboing and countering big groups of goons. In other words, it's fantastic, and younger players should have a ton of fun beating up the bad guys.
See at Steam
Forza Horizon 5 and Forza Horizon 6 (Xbox Series X|S, PC)

You won't be hurling people out of their vehicles so you can take their cars for a joyride, but the Forza Horizon games are fantastic not only for offering best-in-class racing, but also because they have collectibles and activities packed into every nook and cranny of their huge worlds. We specifically recommend Forza Horizon 5 and 6 here, not because they're significantly better than their predecessors, but because they're the only ones you can still purchase digitally. Music rights have meant the other entries have been delisted from various digital storefronts, but both Forza Horizon 5 and Forza Horizon 6 will keep your family entertained for weeks, if not months. Forza Horizon 5 is also available on PlayStation 5 in addition to Xbox and PC, with a similar PS5 release coming for Forza Horizon 6 in early 2027.
See at Steam
Little Kitty, Big City (PS5, PS4, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, Switch, PC, iOS, Android)

Is this big city as big as Vice City? No, but you're playing as a little kitty. After falling from your high-rise apartment's windowsill, you're left figuring out how to get home via puzzles and exploration. It's certainly not going to give you the white-knuckled adrenaline rush you'd get in something like GTA, but for kids--especially younger kids--who want to get into open-ended games, you can do a whole lot worse than Little Kitty, Big City. Of course, you're also free to customize your kitty, so your kids can make them look just like your real-life pet, assuming you have one.
See at Steam
Rockstar Games Presents Table Tennis (Xbox 360 with backwards compatibility)

If you know, you know. Coming off the release of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, Rockstar made Table Tennis. There is no murder in this game, unless you count an absolutely one-sided victory against your opponent in ping-pong. While it had fans scratching their heads at launch because of how unexpected it was from a studio known for open-world crime, Table Tennis is actually an extremely fun game that would be a blast for parents and kids to play together. You could make it a unique double feature, with a Forrest Gump viewing as the appetizer--though you'd probably have to skip all the Vietnam stuff, so you'd see Tom Hanks going directly from playing college football to winning the big ping-pong championship in China. And that's all I have to say about that.
See at Xbox Store
Everything (PS4, Switch, PC)

For years, people have said you can do practically "everything" in Grand Theft Auto, but there exists a game already that lets you be everything: Everything. You can be your favorite animal, something as giant as a planet, or something tiny and microscopic. You're free to do pretty much whatever you want within this framework, and though it certainly doesn't have the story or characters you'd get from a more traditional open-world experience, you can spend hours and hours exploring and discovering cool new things to control.
See at Steam
Mario Kart World (Switch 2)

The first game in franchise history to feature an open world, Mario Kart World combines traditional races with a quirky and secret-filled map to explore. It's pretty enormous, filled with characters who you can watch travel, work, and chill, and it's awesome to be able to see just how all the different racetracks actually connect to each other. With tons of costumes and other bonuses to unlock through racing, exploring, and completing challenges, it's sure to keep your kids busy for a long time--and of course, it's one of the best local multiplayer experiences there is.
See at Nintendo eShop
Untitled Goose Game (PS4, Xbox One, Switch, PC)

One of the most enjoyable things you can do in Grand Theft Auto is mess with random people, whether it be on the streets of Los Santos or the beaches of Vice City. Untitled Goose Game puts you in the webbed feet of a very annoying goose who seems to want nothing more than to ruin someone's day. You're tasked with finding creative ways to do this, and they range from stealing stuff to just tossing someone's lunch in a pond. It's a whole lot milder than what you'd see in a GTA game, especially when it comes to the reactions from the human victims. In Untitled Goose Game, they'll just wonder how their day got so bad, but in GTA, they might try to kill you.
See at Steam
Goat Simulator 3 (PS5, PS4, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, PC)

If Untitled Goose Game doesn't provide enough mayhem and destruction for your family's liking, perhaps we can interest you in Goat Simulator 3? The sequel to Goat Simulator (you didn't miss it--there is no Goat Simulator 2), the premise seems like a joke, but that's exactly why it's so entertaining. As a goat, it's your job to basically ruin the lives of everyone around you, whether that be by ramming into them at full speed or completely wrecking what they're working on. You can also just go wild like you're playing the weirdest version of Tony Hawk's Pro Skater ever made, leaping or launching yourself into the air and trying to see how you can break a game that seems designed to be broken.
See at Steam
No Man's Sky (PS5, PS4, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, Switch 2, Switch, PC, iOS)

In terms of vastness, few games are going to compare to Grand Theft Auto VI when it comes out … but there is at least one that definitely beats it. No Man's Sky was released over a decade ago and has gradually turned into one of the most feature-rich and impressive open-world (or perhaps open-universe) games of all time. You're free to venture essentially anywhere, landing your ship on foreign planets before exploring to research their flora and fauna. Though it was initially a single-player experience, a robust multiplayer component is now included, and thanks to cross-play, it doesn't even matter what system you have if you want to play with a friend or family member somewhere else.
See at Steam

articles.headline: Fireworks says you’re wasting money on AI unless you’re using all the models
keyFacts: Fireworks AI VP Rob Ferguson said companies waste money running AI models on-premise or relying on a single model.
Fireworks AI operates a platform that evaluates tasks and routes them to optimal AI models to maximize efficiency.
Ferguson claimed that routing tasks across multiple models can reduce a company's AI bill by at least 50 percent.
body: Fireworks AI is fine with helping companies run AI models in their own datacenters, though VP Rob Ferguson argues against doing so.

Ferguson told The Register in an interview that while Fireworks AI, a managed inference provider, supports on-prem AI, "we're trying to push people more and more away from it because frankly, it's just the economics."
The GPU hardware is just so expensive that if you can't keep it fully utilized, it's a waste of money, he contends. Ten thousand GPUs, he said, represent a billion dollars of capital.
"You don't want those things to be sitting idle," he said.

For companies with particularly sensitive workloads, Ferguson said, Fireworks is happy to work something out – it offers a service called Sovereign for just that purpose and it has partners like Microsoft that can help. But most inference work probably doesn't need that level of protection, he said.

"The state of the art for everyone is to have a portfolio of models," he explained. "In fact, I think most people don't know that the best model in the world's not Astra. The best model in the world's not Fable. The best model is literally a portfolio and we can prove it. You are always better routing between a few models than to do one singular model."

That's what Fireworks does through Nexus and its API, alongside competitors like Together AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra. As a managed inference platform, Fireworks AI routes inference tasks to whichever model, frontier model subscription, or API is best suited to handle them.
But the company is not just doing naive routing like an AI gateway. It's evaluating tasks as they come in and directing them to the optimal model.

"We build custom routers," Ferguson explained. "Our auto model is continuously updating so that we actually go through and we grade the difficulty of the task and we see if there're affinities that the models have, like Kimi is slightly better at JavaScript than Python, things like this."
The company's competitive edge, he contends, is its crack engineering team, which follows from its founders' work on PyTorch, a widely used open source machine learning library.

"We're performance experts both on the training and inference side," he explained. "People I think don't understand how important, for example, numerics is. So when you use a model, it's always called a mixture of experts – an expert is a different machine.

"And so you have all these different machines. It actually matters when you're training that you go back to precisely the right machine, because if you don't, the other machine will still answer the question, but it'll answer in a slightly different way. So we have to know how to build the topology to write back the data to the right space. We have to understand floating point precision [to handle very small values]. We have to be able to do all this where we're routing through a complex fabric through potentially more than one provider depending on what everything is. And so we're really systems experts."

Hyperscalers, he argues, will give you a GPU but then it's your responsibility to put it to use. Fireworks' advantage involves being able to maximize utilization at scale while maintaining model precision and speed.
Ferguson said AI keeps coming back to economics.

"People are just trying to figure out more and more things to use AI for and [to answer questions like] just how much more can I send to cached models, how much more can I send to open models, when do I need this specialization?" he said. "So we're constantly working with customers to help them come up with their own evaluation criteria."

One reason for this, Ferguson explained, is that frontier model companies are not transparent about their caching rates. He said Fireworks was working with a data science company and was caching about 90 percent of the tasks.

"We looked at [Anthropic's] Opus and it was caching 30 percent of the time," he said. "It was doing AI rework constantly. And with AI, rework is by far your biggest cost. If it's not hitting a cache, then your costs are absolutely insane. And so the token cost is not the real cost. It's the cost per task. And they're hiding that from you. And so we always tell our customers to be tracking cost per task, because that's the real number."
Another factor that companies should consider in their cost calculations, Ferguson suggested, is the value of their data and whether they're giving that data away for training.
"I think people grossly underestimate the value of their data," he said.

Fireworks AI has a zero data-retention policy, "but a lot of times," Ferguson said, "these other companies [do] not, and you should be getting paid for your data. Nobody really knew at the beginning of this current era that these models are memorizers. But now there's plenty of evidence that these models are. So if they're going to be using your data, then you should be getting value for it."
But it's not just about cost. Speed, said Ferguson, is underappreciated.

"Speed is the thing that people often don't know they can ask for," he said. "It's such a game changer for me and how I work with AI is so different when the responses come back as fast as I ask them."
What's the advantage of model ensembling, as the company refers to its model routing activities? A bill that's at least 50 percent smaller, Ferguson claims.

"So we say six to eight times cheaper," he said. "The reality is that because a lot of folks have a preference in their tooling, we kinda guarantee that in the case where you're still using a combo of closed and open models, we can always guarantee that your bill will drop by half right away. Like we're sure about that. And then the question is can we just get you to use more stuff?" ®

articles.headline: How Democrats can make good on their new mandate
keyFacts: Maryland Governor Wes Moore won reelection with roughly 63 percent of the vote following Democratic victories in the midterms.
Moore, considered a potential 2028 presidential candidate, stated Democrats must act fast to address voters' cost of living concerns.
Moore said the incoming Democratic Congress should act within its first hundred hours to stop funding the war in Iran.
body: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down. | Monica Morgan/Getty Images

The midterm elections were great for Democrats everywhere, but some triumphed even more decisively than others: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, for example, cruised to reelection with roughly 63 percent of the vote.

Voters pushed Republicans out — and kept Democrats like Moore in power — in part because of their concerns over a handful of critical issues, including the rising cost of living, the Iran war, and the growing dominance of AI and data centers. The question now is how Democrats can best wield their new power to act on the currents that carried them into office.
For Moore, the stakes may be particularly high: He’s often mentioned as a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2028, speculation that he has not exactly batted down .

America, Actually host Astead Herndon spoke with Moore about his vision for how the Democrats should proceed. As Moore put it, this is a moment in which the party will have to move quickly on the problems that motivate voters most.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel .
Lowering cost is the top priority for voters, and, frankly, it was where they penalized Trump the most. What’s the single biggest thing Democrats could do to address folks’ cost of living concerns?

Actually move fast to fix the things. No more studies. No more 10-year research reports. Move fast. For example, in Maryland, we’ve done permitting reform to be able to speed up affordable housing, right? And I did not need a 10-year research paper to tell me that we have an issue with affordable housing.
Get more housing around transit. Do more transit-oriented development. If it’s state-owned land, don’t tell me why we can’t do something. It is state owned land. Do something on it.

The reason we made the largest investments in childcare in our state’s history is because it is insane when you’re watching the fact that people are spending thirty and forty percent of their paychecks on child care and knowing how much that’s actually going to impact [them]. So there are things that we can do right now to be able to address it.

But I also think that there are things that we need Washington to be able to do. For example, gas prices: There’s no governor that can impact gas prices. We just need to stop fighting stupid wars. There’s no governor that is impacting national energy policy or national grocery prices. What we need to do is stop allowing illegal tariff policy to happen. So I do think that there are things that Washington Democrats have got to do, and that they need to move fast on. But I also think that we don’t need to wait for them to be able to put things in place that we know that actually work.
I wonder what universal healthcare means to you. Is that the government providing insurance?

If you look at what we’ve done here in Maryland, we’ve been able to actually come up with platforms through our Total Cost of Care [Model]. We’re actually working with our hospitals. Our hospitals have a universal budget, and are then able to make sure that people are getting the care that they need.

That has done a tremendous job of being able to help to break the cost curve. Maryland is one of the only states in the country where you’re watching the cost of healthcare actually go down, [while] also being able to increase coverage.

A lot of the Democrats’ affordability message came out of Mamdani’s win. I remember him telling me the one thing he would never budge on is the belief that billionaires shouldn’t exist. I wanted to pose that question to you. Do you think billionaires should exist?

I lose no sleep over the amount of billionaires in our society. I do lose sleep over the amount of children that are growing up in poverty. And I think those who [do] have, have a responsibility to support and uplift and create pathways for those who do not.

Here in our state, we actually cut taxes for the middle class. We cut taxes for military veterans. And I said [to wealthy Marylanders], you need to invest more to make sure that we’re doing things like we’re doing: having the fastest public safety turnaround story in the United States of America, having math and reading scores in our public schools now at five-year highs. And I did ask wealthy Marylanders to invest a little bit more to make sure we can get those kinds of results.

I wanted to move on to Iran. You served in Afghanistan and are a veteran. When we think about this incoming Democratic Congress, should they continue funding a war that Americans have mostly found is not in their interest?
No, and they shouldn’t have funded in the first place.
I’ve heard the argument that that leaves soldiers behind.

No, because we’re talking about a president who unilaterally went to war without even asking Congress for authority. The president does not have the authority to just wage war by himself. That is something that the Constitution lays out. Congress is the only one that has the authority for that. And truthfully, this Congress has been so caught up in the aura of the president of the United States that they have not been leaders; they have been cheerleaders.

Part of the issue is that this Congress needs to be held to account, and that’s exactly what I think happened on Tuesday. But I think about my experiences, right? I served in Afghanistan. I led soldiers with the 82nd Airborne Division, and we went over there with what we believed was an understanding of what was at stake and what needed to happen. That this was about the Taliban, and the Taliban could not be in charge of Afghanistan after 9/11. Twenty years later, trillions of dollars spent, thousands of American service members dead, and do you know who’s in charge of Afghanistan right now? The Taliban.

And so we are dragging ourselves again into another forever war. And the problem is that we have a Congress that is not actually asserting its authority to be able to check this administration. I think that Congress needs to get this done not in the first hundred days, [but] in the first hundred hours. Congress needs to assert its authority and say to the president of the United States: This needs to end.
Data centers also had a horrible night on Tuesday. But I still hear a lot of Democrats say that AI has a place in the economy of tomorrow. Is there a place for pro-AI Democrats in this big tent?

I am very concerned about what we’ve seen from AI, and I know a lot of Americans are. I’m hopeful for what I think the promise of what AI can bring to things like health care and what I think AI can bring to things like education. But I also know that there need to be guardrails.
What we have seen from Donald Trump and these folks is that there are no guardrails. They just let it do what it does. I don’t think that’s the right answer. I think that’s remarkably dangerous.

I don’t think that the answer is telling them, “Police yourself, guys, because that’s going to get us to the right answer.” And that’s why in Maryland, we’ve actually put together guidelines as to how we’re going to be protected from AI. That includes things like protecting our workforce. That includes things like protecting our pocketbooks. That includes things like protecting our children.

We put together some of the most stringent guidelines in the country that said things like, they have to pay for all their own energy and all their own upgrades. That our taxpayers do not pay a single penny for that. That they cannot pollute our air or pollute our water. They need to follow all environmental guidelines. That they need to hire local union workers. And also really importantly, that we need to make sure that the people of Maryland have control, not the data center companies, not the Trump administration. That control belongs to us.

About half of the local jurisdictions in Maryland have either a ban or a pause on [data centers]. And I’ve said the state will never override you, ever. If you have a ban or a pause, that is done, because control goes to the locals.

articles.headline: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
keyFacts: Bantu speakers began expanding across southern Africa thousands of years ago, introducing farming, livestock, pottery, and metalworking.
Archaeometallurgist Ezekiel Mtetwa said ancient furnace discoveries in southern Africa indicate intensive and technologically sophisticated iron production.
The Bantu expansion transformed the continent's culture, leaving roughly 350 million people speaking Bantu languages today.
body: It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters.

At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors.

Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.

“The number and size of these furnaces, together with the use of natural-draft technology, indicate intensive and technologically sophisticated iron production,” says archaeometallurgist Ezekiel Mtetwa of Chicago’s Field Museum of Natural History, who has long studied the furnaces.

Scientists are extremely interested in the peoples who created this and other iron-powered societies across eastern and southern Africa. Research points to an adaptable and innovative group from western Africa as the masterminds. Known as Bantu speakers, these communities began gradually expanding across the continent’s southern half, starting from 6,000 to 4,000 years ago. In doing so, they introduced a fundamentally new, sedentary way of life—characterized by farming, raising livestock, pottery-making, and metalworking—to regions previously dominated by hunter-gatherer communities.

This migration transformed not only the region’s history and technology, but also its languages: Today, around 350 million Africans speak one of roughly 500 distinct Bantu tongues, from southern African Zulu to eastern African Swahili. And at least as many Africans—as well as many African Americans and Afro-Latinos—carry Bantu ancestry in their DNA.

articles.headline: Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get
keyFacts: Alpine Linux and other musl-based distributions have an OpenSSH authentication bypass vulnerability caused by a C library error handling flaw.
Attackers can log into key-only accounts by sending a specific length password if certain default configurations are enabled.
Alpine released patched software versions, and administrators must upgrade packages and restart the SSH daemon immediately.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- An ancient bug is affecting Alpine Linux and a few other Linux distros.
- It’s about as bad as it can get.
- You must patch ASAP, and then restart the patched software.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.
How the attack works
As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:
Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.
That’s it. That’s all.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant, and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.
In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.
According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.
Who’s exposed
Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:
- The openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no.
- PasswordAuthentication set to yes, which is the OpenSSH default.
- An account with * as its password field, and another account with a 5 or 6 hash.

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.
Alpine said these are not affected:
- Containers that do not run sshd.
- Systems with password authentication disabled.
- Systems using openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes.
- Locked accounts with! in the password field.
- Cloud images configured through cloud-init, which writes PasswordAuthentication no.
The fix

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.
